abstract: |
  A tail model that fits a heavy-tailed family (GPD, log-logistic) to storm
  mortality can produce an infinite or near-infinite estimated mean when the
  fitted shape implies a tail index $\alpha \le 1$ ($\xi \ge 1$), even though the
  outcome is physically bounded (deaths cannot exceed the exposed population).
  This document reviews the three principled routes to a finite, well-behaved
  mean under a *known* upper bound: (A) the Cirillo--Taleb dual-distribution
  "shadow mean"; (B) a renormalised truncated likelihood in the sense of Aban,
  Meerschaert & Panorska; and (C) censoring at the physical cap. It derives the
  estimator and mean for each, states the assumptions each makes about the
  unobserved region between the data and the cap, and locates the present
  application within the soft- vs. hard-truncation taxonomy of Chakrabarty &
  Samorodnitsky. The central conclusion is that the storm-mortality problem sits
  in the *hard*-truncation regime, where the physical bound materially reshapes
  the tail and a finite mean is stable and data-supported --- the regime in which
  (B) and (C) are appropriate and the dual transform (A), a soft-regime tool, is
  the sensitivity probe rather than the default.

# The problem {#sec-problem}

## Setup and notation {#sec-notation}

Let each storm $i$ contribute an observed death count $D_i$ and an exposure
$E_i$. In the `idd-tc-mortality` pipeline the modelled quantity is a **rate**

$$
r_i = \frac{D_i}{E_i},
$$ {#eq-rate}

where $E_i$ is *person--storm--hours* (PSH), not a simple headcount. A separate
column, `exposed_population` $= P_i$, records the number of people exposed. The
physical constraint is $D_i \le P_i$: a storm cannot kill more people than are
present. Expressed on the rate scale of @eq-rate this becomes a **storm-specific
upper bound**

$$
r_i \;\le\; c_i \;=\; \frac{P_i}{E_i},
$$ {#eq-cap}

which varies across storms because the ratio of headcount to person--storm--hours
depends on storm duration and exposure geometry. The tail stage is fit on the
**excess rate** over a threshold $u$ (`threshold_rate`),

$$
w_i = r_i - u \ge 0,
$$ {#eq-excess}

and the threshold is added back at prediction time. Because the excess-rate
families are defined with support beginning at $0$, we have $F(0)=0$ for every
family; there is no left-truncation term to carry. The cap on the excess scale is
$c_i - u$.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two scales must be reconciled

The threshold $u$ is defined historically in rate-per-PSH units, and the cap
$c_i = P_i/E_i$ is *also* a rate-per-PSH quantity (it is the rate at which the
entire exposed population dies). Both therefore live in the same space and the
truncation quantity $F(c_i - u) - F(0) = F(c_i - u)$ is coherent. This
reconciliation is *only* automatic because the cap is expressed as $P_i/E_i$ on
the same rate scale as $u$; naively capping a *fraction* $D_i/P_i$ at $1$ while
thresholding a *rate* $D_i/E_i$ would mix two scales and silently corrupt the
normaliser.
:::

## Why an unbounded fit gives an infinite mean {#sec-infinite}

A generalized Pareto tail has survival function
$\bar F(w) = (1 + \xi w/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}$ and, writing $\alpha = 1/\xi$, its
$p$-th moment is finite **iff** $\xi < 1/p$, equivalently $\alpha > p$
[@embrechts1997modelling; @dehaan2006extreme]. Thus the mean exists only for
$\xi < 1$ ($\alpha > 1$). The log-logistic AFT tail behaves identically: with
shape $k$ its mean is undefined for $k \le 1$. When the fitted tail index sits at
$\alpha \approx 0.7$ (so $\xi \approx 1.43$), the fitted latent distribution has
**no finite first moment**. A point prediction from such a fit is necessarily a
*median* (or another low quantile), because that is the only central summary that
exists --- which is exactly what the current pipeline reports for its MLE'd
AFT/EVT families.

The consequence for evaluation is structural, not cosmetic: an out-of-sample
target formed by summing observed deaths is a finite, mean-like quantity, but the
predicted central value from an $\alpha \le 1$ fit corresponds to a median. Any
ratio-style calibration gate then compares a mean-like numerator to a median-like
denominator, and for a right-skewed tail the median is far below the mean. This
is the mechanism by which the downstream super-region "rake" acquires its
load-bearing role: it is silently repairing a mean/median mismatch created
upstream.

::: {.callout-note}
## The bound dissolves the paradox

A distribution with **bounded support has finite moments of all orders**,
regardless of how heavy the tail *looks* over the observed range
[@cirillo2020tail]. The apparent infinite mean is an artefact of extrapolating an
unbounded family past a bound that in fact exists. Every method below is a
different disciplined way of imposing that bound; they differ in *how* they treat
the unobserved region between the largest observation and the cap.
:::

## The data geometry that decides everything {#sec-geometry}

The largest observed per-capita death fraction in the storm data is
$\max_i D_i/P_i \approx 0.2$; roughly $70\%$ of storms have zero deaths and are
handled upstream by the hurdle stages. The cap in fraction terms is $1$, so the
observed data reach only about one-fifth of the way to the cap, and the two
catastrophic storms that dominate the death total (2008 Nargis; 1991 Bangladesh /
Gorky) are *not* the maxima on the per-capita fraction scale --- they are extreme
in absolute deaths, not in fraction of exposed. The unobserved region on the
fraction scale spans roughly $[0.2,\,1]$, i.e. under one order of magnitude. As
@sec-regime shows, this "how far is the cap from the data" ratio is the single
quantity that determines which method is appropriate.

# Method A --- the dual-distribution shadow mean {#sec-A}

## Construction {#sec-A-construction}

@taleb2016shadow and @cirillo2020tail address exactly the apparent-infinite-mean
problem, motivated by war casualties [@cirillo2016statistical], operational risk
[@cirillo2016expected], and pandemic fatalities [@cirillo2020tail]. Rather than
truncate, they **transform the bounded variable to an unbounded one**, fit
ordinary extreme-value theory (EVT) there, and transform back. For a variable $Y$
on support $[L, H]$ define the log-transform

$$
\varphi(Y) = L - H \log\!\left(\frac{H - Y}{H - L}\right).
$$ {#eq-dual}

This map is $C^\infty$, parameter-free, satisfies $\varphi^{-1}(\infty) = H$ and
$\varphi(L) = L$, and for $Y \ll H$ gives $\varphi(Y) \approx Y$. The transformed
("dual") variable $Z = \varphi(Y)$ has support $[L, \infty)$, so it may legitimately
be modelled in the Fréchet class and a GPD fitted to its exceedances via the
Pickands--Balkema--de Haan theorem. Because $\varphi$ is one-to-one and
parameter-free, the GPD shape $\xi$ estimated on the dual data equals the shape of
the raw tail up to the point where the bound bends the real tail down
[@cirillo2020tail]. One then reverts to $Y$ and computes the **shadow mean** --- a
conditional (tail) expectation that is finite even when the raw fit suggests
$\xi > 1$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Y > L^\ast]
= (H - L)\, e^{\frac{1}{\xi}\frac{\sigma}{H}}
  \left(\frac{\sigma}{H\xi}\right)^{\!1/\xi}
  \Gamma\!\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\xi},\, \tfrac{\sigma}{H\xi}\right) + L,
$$ {#eq-shadowmean}

with $\Gamma(\cdot,\cdot)$ the upper incomplete Gamma function. The paper also
gives closed forms for the quantile function, Value-at-Risk, and Expected
Shortfall by the same route.

## The comparison to hard truncation, in the authors' own terms {#sec-A-vs-trunc}

@taleb2016shadow explicitly contrasts the dual transform with three alternatives:
(i) hard truncation with renormalisation (Method B below); (ii) an absorbing
barrier that piles the excess mass as a Dirac atom at $H$ (Method C below); and
(iii) the dual transform. Their central objection to (i) and (ii) is
*smoothness*: hard truncation creates a "cliff" --- an abrupt end of density at
$H$ --- and risk measures on non-smooth densities are unstable. Their Figure 2
shows that the truncated-Pareto mean and the smooth-transform mean **diverge most
strongly for $\alpha < 1$**, with the smooth mean lower. The dual transform's
real tail bends smoothly toward $H$ rather than continuing as a straight power law
that is then guillotined.

## The storm-specific-$H$ problem {#sec-A-covariates}

For a *marginal* fit (no covariates) with a single global $H$ --- the pandemic
case, where $H$ is world population --- the transform is a single fixed function
and its properties (shape invariance, clean back-transform) hold globally. In the
storm application $H_i = c_i - u$ is **storm-specific**, so $\varphi_i$ is a
different nonlinear map for each storm. Two consequences follow.

1. **The dual variables are not identically distributed** unless one first
   rescales to a common bound. The clean fix is to transform the
   *fraction-of-cap* $g_i = w_i/(c_i - u) \in (0,1]$ with a common $H = 1$, pool
   the duals, fit one GPD, and recover per-storm shadow means by rescaling by
   $(c_i - u)$.
2. **Covariates cannot enter cleanly.** Because $H_i$ is built from $P_i$ and
   $E_i$ --- quantities correlated with any plausible intensity covariate ---
   putting a covariate on the dual scale entangles the coefficient with the
   transform geometry and risks confounding with exposure. Method A is therefore
   run **without covariates**, as a marginal reference, not as a covariate model.

::: {.callout-caution}
## When A earns its complexity

The dual transform is a *soft-regime* instrument (@sec-regime): it is designed for
the case where the cap $H$ is orders of magnitude above the data and the mean is
dominated by the vast unobserved gap, so a defensible *shape* through that gap is
essential. Its downward bend near $H$ is an imposed modelling choice, not a
data-estimated feature; it is "more principled" than a straight extrapolation only
to the extent that the true process actually bends. When the gap is short
(@sec-geometry), A and a straight truncation nearly coincide and the transform
buys little.
:::

# Method B --- renormalised truncated likelihood {#sec-B}

## Construction {#sec-B-construction}

Method B is the classical **upper-truncated maximum-likelihood** estimator. For a
family with density $f(\cdot;\theta)$ and CDF $F(\cdot;\theta)$ on $[0,\infty)$,
restrict the support to $(0,\, c_i - u]$ and renormalise so the density integrates
to one over that interval. The per-storm log-likelihood contribution is

$$
\ell_i(\theta)
= \log f(w_i;\theta_i) - \log F(c_i - u;\, \theta_i),
$$ {#eq-B-loglik}

with $\theta_i$ carrying covariates through, e.g., $\sigma_i = \exp(x_i^\top\beta)$.
(The $-\log[F(c_i-u) - F(0)]$ of the general doubly-truncated form collapses to
$-\log F(c_i-u)$ because $F(0)=0$ on the excess scale.) This is precisely the
estimator of @aban2006parameter, who derived the MLE for the truncated-Pareto tail
index with right-truncation point $T$ and showed the @hill1975simple estimator is
its $T \to \infty$ limit. With known bounds the MLE has the usual regularity
properties. Method B here generalises it to a family sweep and a covariate layer.

The truncated **mean** used for scoring is

$$
\mathbb{E}[w \mid 0 < w \le c_i - u]
= \frac{\displaystyle\int_0^{c_i - u} w\, f(w;\theta_i)\, dw}{F(c_i - u;\theta_i)},
$$ {#eq-B-mean}

closed-form for the GPD via the upper incomplete Gamma function and for the
log-logistic via the incomplete Beta function; add back $u$ and multiply by $E_i$
to recover expected deaths.

## Cost and identifiability {#sec-B-cost}

With covariates the normaliser $F(c_i - u;\theta_i)$ depends on $\beta$ both
through the argument and through $\sigma_i$, so it contributes a **distinct
closed-form term per storm to every gradient evaluation**. This does not require
numerical differentiation --- the score is analytic --- but it does not collapse to
a shared-parameter expression the way the no-covariate case does. The practical
costs are therefore (i) a per-storm sum inside each gradient step, mitigated by
hand-coding the analytic score and warm-starting from the untruncated fit, and
(ii) a genuinely more serious concern flagged by @beirlant2016tail: under
**hard** truncation the tail-index estimate can become weakly identified, because
one is estimating a power-law exponent from data squeezed against a nearby ceiling
and the likelihood can be flat in $\xi$. @beirlant2016tail and
@beirlant2017fitting propose a truncated-Pareto QQ-plot and a formal test for
truncation precisely to diagnose this.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Back-out criterion for B is not only wall-clock

Because B's real risk is a flat/unstable $\xi$ rather than merely slow
optimisation, the abort signal should include near-flat identifiability (a very
large standard error on $\xi$, or an optimiser that wanders) as well as an
iteration/time budget. When B is unstable, C is the graceful fallback.
:::

# Method C --- censoring at the physical cap {#sec-C}

## Construction {#sec-C-construction}

Method C treats the latent lethality as an *unbounded* heavy-tailed process whose
*observed* outcome is capped: $\tilde r_i = \min(r_i,\, c_i)$. The interior
density is left exactly as the untruncated family (no renormalisation), and the
mass the family assigns above the cap is collected into an atom at $c_i$:

$$
\ell_i(\theta) =
\begin{cases}
\log f(w_i;\theta_i), & w_i < c_i - u \quad(\text{interior}),\\[4pt]
\log\!\big[\,1 - F(c_i - u;\theta_i)\,\big], & w_i = c_i - u \quad(\text{at cap}).
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-C-loglik}

There is **no normaliser on the interior** (the excess-scale density already
integrates correctly from $0$; there is no $1 - F(0)$ term since $F(0)=0$). The
interior likelihood is therefore *identical to the untruncated fit*. This is the
"absorbing barrier / Dirac atom at $H$" option of @taleb2016shadow and the
actuarial upper-truncated treatment of @clark2013note.

The relevant **mean** is the censored expectation, finite for any tail heaviness
because the integrand is capped:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\min(w,\, c_i - u)\big]
= \int_0^{c_i - u} w\, f(w;\theta_i)\, dw
  + (c_i - u)\big[\,1 - F(c_i - u;\theta_i)\,\big].
$$ {#eq-C-mean}

## Why C is the cheap route to a finite mean {#sec-C-cheap}

Two facts combine. First, the interior likelihood equals the untruncated
likelihood, so C reuses existing fast machinery for the fit --- there is no
per-storm normaliser in the gradient. Second, in the present data **no storm sits
at its cap** (@sec-geometry): with the atom rule set to exact equality
$D_i = P_i$ and $\max_i D_i/P_i \approx 0.2$, the atom set is empty. The atom term
of @eq-C-loglik therefore contributes nothing in-sample, and C's *fit* is exactly
the untruncated fit. C differs from the (broken) untruncated method **only at
prediction/scoring time**, where @eq-C-mean caps the predictive integral at $c_i$
and so returns a finite mean where the untruncated integral diverges.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The practical upshot

For the heavy families (GPD, log-logistic) C delivers a finite mean at the cost of
an ordinary fit plus a one-time censored-mean integral. For the light,
already-finite-mean families the censored mean $\approx$ the ordinary mean (the
mass above $c_i$ is negligible), so C offers nothing over the naive fit and need
not be built for them. C is thus the natural workhorse for the two families that
have the infinite-mean pathology, and only those.
:::

## What C assumes {#sec-C-assumes}

C does not escape the unobserved-gap problem; it *relocates* it. The censored mean
in @eq-C-mean is trustworthy to the extent that either the data reach the cap
neighbourhood or the tail is light enough that the region $[\,\max_i w_i,\, c_i - u\,]$
contributes little. When the fitted tail is heavy, a large share of @eq-C-mean
comes from the atom term $(c_i - u)[1 - F(c_i - u)]$, whose mass is an
extrapolation no observation constrains. The straight power-law extrapolation of C
and the bent extrapolation of A (@sec-A-vs-trunc) disagree exactly over this gap,
and the disagreement grows with $\xi$; their spread is the diagnostic of how
assumption-driven the mean is (@sec-diagnostics).

# The soft/hard-truncation taxonomy: which method for which world {#sec-regime}

The result that organises the whole choice is @chakrabarty2012understanding, "Is a
truncated heavy tail heavy or not?" They define two regimes by the position of the
truncation point relative to the sample:

- In the **soft-truncation regime** the cap is so far above the bulk of the data
  that truncated power tails behave, in important respects, *as if no truncation
  took place*. The characteristic heavy-tail behaviour is retained; the mean is
  dominated by the large unobserved region above the data.
- In the **hard-truncation regime** the cap is close enough to the data that much
  of the "heavy-tailedness" is lost. Truncation materially reshapes the tail; the
  finite mean is stable and supported by the data rather than by extrapolation.

They also give consistent estimators of the tail exponent under truncation and a
test to decide which regime obtains.

## Locating the storm problem {#sec-regime-locate}

With $\max_i D_i/P_i \approx 0.2$ and a fraction cap of $1$, the cap sits at roughly
$5\times$ the largest observation --- under one order of magnitude. This is the
**hard**-truncation regime. Two conclusions follow, and they invert the naive
"defer to the sophisticated method" instinct:

1. Because truncation materially reshapes the tail, it **cannot be ignored**: the
   physical bound is doing real work, and methods that impose it (B, C) are
   appropriate. Simultaneously, because much heavy-tailedness is lost, the finite
   mean is **stable and data-supported**, not a knife-edge extrapolation.
2. The dual transform (A) is a soft-regime tool. Its elaborate machinery earns its
   keep only when the gap spans orders of magnitude and dominates the mean --- the
   pandemic case, not the storm case. Over the short storm gap, A's bent
   extrapolation and C's straight one nearly coincide, so A collapses toward being
   a sensitivity check rather than the default.

::: {.callout-important}
## The pandemic case is the opposite regime

@cirillo2020tail fit pandemics with $\xi \approx 1.62$ and a cap (world
population, $\sim\!10^{9}$--$10^{10}$) some two orders of magnitude above the
largest observation ($\sim\!10^{8}$). That is deep in the **soft** regime, where
censoring at the cap does almost nothing (the survival at $H$ is negligible) and
the entire mean lives in the unobserved $[\,M, H\,]$ gap. The dual transform was
built for that situation. Reading its rhetorical conclusion --- that sample means
are "meaningless" and compartmental point estimates unfit for risk --- as a general
law rather than a soft-regime, worst-case-risk-management statement over-generalises
it to a regime (hard truncation, calibrated central estimation) it was not written
for.
:::

## The negative-shape shortcut does not work {#sec-regime-negshape}

One might hope to avoid explicit truncation by letting the tail fit choose a
bounded shape --- a GPD with $\xi < 0$ has a finite right endpoint. @beirlant2016tail
found that standard EVT methods, **even with a negative extreme-value index, fail
to capture truncation at high levels**: the fitted endpoint of a negative-$\xi$ GPD
does not coincide with the known physical cap $c_i$. Imposing the *known* bound
explicitly (B or C) is therefore necessary; shape flexibility alone will not
recover it.

# Comparison and expected behaviour {#sec-comparison}

## The bias ordering {#sec-ordering}

@aban2006parameter's precipitation application reports the empirical ordering that
should be expected here too: for extreme upper quantiles the fully-truncated model
gives the *lowest* estimate, and the untruncated-but-cap-aware version the
*highest*, with intermediate treatments between. Translated to the present
methods, the expected ordering of central tail estimates is

$$
\underbrace{\text{B (renormalised)}}_{\text{lowest}}
\;\le\;
\underbrace{\text{C (censored)}}_{\text{middle}}
\;\le\;
\underbrace{\text{D (untruncated, finite-mean families)}}_{\text{highest}},
$$ {#eq-ordering}

with A anywhere but, in the soft regime it is built for, typically high. B pulls
the tail down most because renormalisation removes the above-cap mass and
redistributes it inward, lightening the fitted tail; C retains more weight by
keeping the untruncated interior and lodging the residual mass at the cap. If the
downstream evidence indicates the model needs a *higher* central tail to match
observed totals --- which the documented under-prediction and the corrective rake
suggest --- then @eq-ordering predicts C will tend to beat B.

## Summary table {#sec-table}

| Aspect | A: Dual / shadow mean | B: Renormalised truncation | C: Censoring at cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Provenance | @taleb2016shadow; @cirillo2020tail | @aban2006parameter; @hill1975simple limit | @taleb2016shadow (atom option); @clark2013note |
| What it does to above-cap mass | bends tail smoothly toward $H$ via transform | redistributes it inward (renormalise) | lodges it as an atom at the cap |
| Fit cost | trivial (marginal, no covariates) | high (per-storm normaliser in gradient) | low (interior = untruncated fit) |
| Covariates | no (storm-specific $H$ confounds) | yes (clean, on latent scale) | yes (clean, on latent scale) |
| Mean | @eq-shadowmean | @eq-B-mean | @eq-C-mean |
| Finite mean at $\xi>1$? | yes | yes | yes |
| Right regime | soft truncation | hard (canonical) | hard (natural) |
| Key risk | bent extrapolation is imposed, not estimated | $\xi$ identifiability under hard truncation | atom mass is unconstrained extrapolation |
| Families to build | GPD, log-logistic | GPD, log-logistic (+ Weibull check) | GPD, log-logistic |

: Side-by-side of the three bounded-mean methods, plus the naive untruncated
baseline D for the already-finite-mean families. {#tbl-compare}

## The role of variant D {#sec-D}

For families with an always-finite mean (gamma, lognormal, truncated-normal,
negative binomial, Poisson, Weibull) the honest baseline is simply to fit them
untruncated and report their ordinary mean --- "what essentially all of applied
statistics does with a Poisson model." This is **variant D**. It exists to
*measure* how much the boundedness correction buys: if a D-family already predicts
the mean well out-of-sample and shrinks the rake toward one, the elaborate
machinery was unnecessary for it. D must not be applied to GPD or log-logistic,
for which "assume infinite support" reproduces the very infinite-mean pathology
the exercise removes. Note that the AFT/EVT families currently report medians;
moving them into a mean-based competition requires converting Weibull (and any
other median-reporting family retained) to return its **mean**, not its median.

# Diagnostics that make the choice empirical {#sec-diagnostics}

Three diagnostics turn the method choice from an argument into a measurement.

1. **A-vs-C mean spread, per family.** Because A (bent) and C (straight) disagree
   only over the unobserved gap, and by an amount that grows with $\xi$, their
   per-storm mean spread measures how far the reported mean is driven by tail-shape
   assumption versus by data. Small spread $\Rightarrow$ the gap is immaterial,
   ship C. Large spread $\Rightarrow$ the mean is assumption-driven and the spread
   itself should be reported as structural uncertainty.
2. **Rake-ratio shrinkage toward one, per variant.** The super-region rake is the
   one place aggregate near-cap information enters the pipeline; it currently
   multiplies predictions to match observed super-region totals. A variant under
   which the rake ratio moves toward one has, by that fact, produced a mean that
   agrees with the aggregate observed data --- the strongest available empirical
   check on the gap extrapolation, short of data in the gap. This is the headline
   "did we fix the under-prediction at source" number.
3. **Truncation identifiability check for B.** Following @beirlant2016tail and
   @beirlant2017fitting, a truncated QQ-plot / truncation test flags when B's
   $\xi$ is weakly identified. This is the concrete abort criterion complementing
   the wall-clock budget (@sec-B-cost).

Out-of-sample scoring must be performed on the **finite mean** each bounded method
produces, so that all candidates --- including the previously median-reporting
AFT/EVT families --- are compared on the same functional. Because every bounded
method has finite moments of all orders, mean-based proper scores (e.g. CRPS on the
bounded predictive) are all admissible; the previous need to fall back on
log-scores to dodge a missing mean no longer applies.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The storm-mortality tail lives in the hard-truncation regime of
@chakrabarty2012understanding: the physical cap sits under an order of magnitude
above the data, materially reshaping the tail and rendering a finite mean stable
and data-supported. In that regime the canonical truncated-MLE of
@aban2006parameter (Method B) and censoring at the cap (Method C) are the
appropriate estimators; C is additionally the cheap one, because with no storm at
its cap its fit coincides with the untruncated fit and only the scoring integral
changes. The Cirillo--Taleb dual transform (Method A) is a soft-regime instrument
whose elaborate, physically-imposed extrapolation earns its keep only when the cap
is remote and the mean is gap-dominated --- the pandemic case, not this one --- so
it is retained as a marginal sensitivity probe rather than as the default. None of
B, C, or A is "obviously horrible": B is textbook with known MLE properties, C is
regime-appropriate and standard, and A is correct for the world it was built for.
The remaining genuine risks are narrow and each has a named diagnostic: B's
$\xi$-identifiability under hard truncation (truncated QQ-test), and the
unconstrained above-cap extrapolation shared by A and C (the A-vs-C spread and the
rake-ratio shrinkage). The recommended posture is to build A, C, and D (all cheap),
read the rake-shrinkage and A-vs-C diagnostics, and treat B as a gated second phase
justified only if C proves insufficient.

# Literature-expansion plan for the manuscript introduction {#sec-expansion}

The synthesis above rests on the roughly ten primary sources actually consulted. A
manuscript-grade introduction should broaden along the following branches, each of
which is a distinct search with its own key sources to locate:

- **Truncated / tempered heavy-tail families as alternatives to hard truncation.**
  Tempered stable and truncated-Lévy-flight models [@meerschaert2004tempered] and
  stretched-exponential fat tails with characteristic scales
  [@laherrere1998stretched] "temper" rather than guillotine the tail --- a fourth
  conceptual option alongside A/B/C worth positioning against. Search terms:
  *tempered Pareto Weibull*, *truncated Lévy flight*, *stretched exponential fat
  tail*.
- **The consistency and asymptotics of truncated-tail estimation.** Beyond
  @aban2006parameter, pull the Hill-under-truncation asymptotic-normality results
  and the trimming approach of Nuyts. Search terms: *asymptotic normality Hill
  estimator truncated*, *Beirlant Reynkens fitting tails truncation*.
- **Actuarial upper-bounded loss modelling.** The reinsurance-cap literature
  (Albrecher, Beirlant & Teugels; @clark2013note) treats known caps as a routine
  feature and is the closest applied analogue to a physical mortality ceiling.
  Search terms: *upper-truncated Pareto reinsurance cap*, *bounded severity
  distribution actuarial*.
- **Truncation forecast from physical models.** Geophysical bounds such as the
  Gutenberg--Richter relation for earthquake magnitude are the natural-science
  precedent for a *known, physically-motivated* cap, exactly analogous to
  $D_i \le P_i$. Search terms: *Gutenberg-Richter truncated magnitude*,
  *physically bounded tail geophysics*.
- **Regression on tail parameters.** The covariate layer (letting $\sigma_i$ or
  the shape depend on covariates) should be grounded in the extreme-value
  regression / GAMLSS-for-extremes literature to justify Methods B and C carrying
  covariates on the latent scale. Search terms: *generalized Pareto regression
  covariates*, *non-stationary extreme value model scale covariate*.
